## Methods to follow clusters over time, not implemented yet

Presented in the guide "Following clusters over time" as possible future
methods. `merge_dynamic_clusters()` has the double majority
(`method = "majority"`) and the Jaccard matching (`method = "jaccard"`).

- **Multislice community detection** (Mucha et al., 2010): detect communities
  in all the windows at once, in a network where each node is tied to itself
  in adjacent windows with a coupling weight $\omega$. Identifiers are shared
  by construction; $\omega$ plays the role of the threshold. Needs nodes
  present in several windows (co-citation, authors, journals rather than
  documents).
- **Significance-clustered alluvial maps** (Rosvall and Bergstrom, 2010):
  bootstrap the network to find which clusters are robust, then draw the flows
  between robust clusters. Addresses the instability of each partition rather
  than the matching rule.
- Record splits and merges as events (one cluster matched to several), which
  the two current rules do not do.
- Compare a cluster with windows older than the previous one (a cluster that
  vanishes for one window and comes back gets a new identifier).

## Alluvial

- `minimize_crossing_alluvial()` is a local search (insertion moves). Ideas:
  several starting orders, simulated annealing, or an order per window
  (barycentre heuristic) instead of one order for all the windows; a measure of
  the crossings in `plot_alluvial()`.

## Naming clusters with a language model

- Reread the documentation of `name_clusters()` (method `"llm"` and its
  arguments) and the code of `R/name_clusters.R` and
  `R/name_clusters_llm.R`.
- Guide "Finding and reading clusters"
  (`vignettes/articles/finding-and-reading-clusters.qmd`): add
  `name_clusters(method = "llm")` to the section "Naming clusters with
  tf-idf", with a chunk `preview = TRUE` (runs without a model) and the call
  with a model in a chunk not evaluated. Place it after "The role of
  documents: hubs and bridges", or point to it, to explain
  `order_by = "within_module_degree"`. What worked on coupling networks
  (Econometrica and Journal of Finance, 27 clusters, `mistral` and
  `ministral-3`): titles, years and the tf-idf label of the 10 nodes with
  the highest within-module degree, about 350 tokens per cluster, right
  cluster found by a judge model for about 6 labels out of 10 (1 out of 13
  by chance); `nb_nodes = 5` almost as good; total degree, PageRank,
  citations or random order worse; abstracts and `nb_nodes = 20` no better;
  the tf-idf label alone about as good.

## Layouts and the hairball (notes of 2026-11-06)

Sources read: Peixoto (2024, blog post, skewed.de/lab/posts/hairball/),
Jacomy (2020, blog post "Hidden structures in hairballs, and how to see them",
Reticular, 2020-10-26), Dianati (2016, *Phys. Rev. E* 93, 012304, accepted
manuscript read up to the start of the GLF section). Other references below
were only checked through a search (title, venue, year), not read: read them
before citing, and add to `inst/REFERENCES.bib` and `references.bib` only then.

### The three positions

- **Jacomy: the hairball is a perception problem, not (only) a layout failure.**
  Gestalt proximity and closure: we see groups because there are *gaps*; a
  force-directed layout puts same-cluster nodes close (a *locality* principle)
  but does not care about gaps (the eye looks at borders, the algorithm at
  barycentres). With a planted partition, the groups are correctly placed but
  touch when P_in approaches P_out (about 60% against 50% in his example): the
  structure is there, not visible. Advice: colour nodes by cluster (or by an
  attribute) and check that colours form coherent localities; look at the
  contour of the map (*poles*: dense zones on the sides pulling the shape);
  rerun a non-deterministic clustering several times: poles are stable,
  boundaries are not, and the ambiguity of the middle is a feature of the data.
  Test on a random network (500 nodes, p = 5%): clusters then map no area.
  Caveat: visual argument only, he states it is not proved; and "high gravity
  produces a hairball whatever the structure" (check the ForceAtlas2 gravity).
- **Peixoto: visualisation second, not first.** A force layout sees only
  assortative structure (random bipartite and tripartite graphs look
  structureless), invites apophenia, and modularity maximisation overfits
  (finds modules in random networks). Proposal: infer the partition with a
  stochastic block model (nested, by description length), then *constrain* the
  layout (extra attraction inside groups with a weight `gamma`, one force per
  hierarchy level, convex hulls); ranked/ordered SBM for networks with a
  latent order (vertical axis = rank). The post says nothing on edge pruning.
  Note the disagreement with Jacomy: for Jacomy the layout is a better
  reduction than hard clusters because it keeps their ambiguity; for Peixoto
  the clusters must come from inference and the layout must obey them.
- **Dianati: prune the edges.** Thresholding on weight discounts low-degree
  nodes. Marginal Likelihood Filter: p-value of each edge weight under a
  null model preserving strengths on average (binomial with
  p = k_i k_j / (2T^2)), keep the smallest p-values: sorting problem, almost
  linear in the number of edges. Global Likelihood Filter (maximum-entropy
  ensemble, Monte Carlo, costly). Distinguishes *pruning* (remove noise to
  reveal an unknown core) from *sparsification* (approximate the graph keeping
  a property). Integer weights only (counts of events).

### What already exists in the package, and how it relates

- `build_network(method = "sdsm" | "fdsm" | "fixed*")` (backbone package)
  already prunes **at construction**, through the bipartite projection null
  models, with `alpha`. This is close to Dianati's logic (null model preserving
  degrees) but applies to projections of a bipartite table. What is missing is
  pruning of an **existing weighted graph** (angle, jaccard... weights are not
  counts, so MLF does not apply directly).
- `layout_networks()`: `"fr"`, `"kk"`, `"forceatlas2"`, `"umap"`, igraph
  layouts, and dynamic coordinates. No gravity/scaling exposed for FA2? (check
  `R/layout_custom.R`), no layout based on a sparsified graph, no layout
  constrained by clusters.
- `add_clusters()` is a single Leiden run (`leiden_workflow`): no stability
  check, no SBM.

### Possible changes to the package (to prioritise with the user)

1. **Layout on a backbone, edges put back for the drawing.** An argument
   `layout_on = "full" | "backbone"` (or a `prune` argument) in
   `layout_networks()`; `graphlayouts::layout_backbone()` and
   `backbone::sparsify.with.quadrilateral()` (Nocaj et al. 2015) already do the
   Simmelian version and `graphlayouts` is an ggraph dependency, so cheap to
   try. Other filters to expose: disparity filter (Serrano et al. 2009),
   MLF (Dianati 2016, easy to write for count weights), maximum spanning tree
   plus top-k edges per node (simple, keeps low-degree nodes).
2. **Cluster-constrained layout** (Peixoto): add an attraction between nodes of
   the same `cluster_id` (strength `gamma`), possibly one level per hierarchy
   level; our own FA2 makes this easy (extra attractive term on same-cluster
   pairs, or extra edges between same-cluster nodes with a small weight, which
   works with any igraph layout). Add hulls around clusters in `plot_networks()`
   (ggforce is already a plausible dependency, check).
3. **Gaps diagnostic.** Quantify Jacomy's point: a measure of how well a layout
   separates clusters visually (e.g. silhouette of the 2D coordinates by
   cluster, or the ratio between within-cluster and nearest-other-cluster
   distances, border to border rather than centroid to centroid), returned with
   `layout_networks()` or by a `check_layout()` helper; useful to compare `fr`,
   `forceatlas2`, `umap`. The guide "Drawing networks" already compares three
   layouts by eye.
4. **Clustering stability** (Jacomy's reruns; Rosvall and Bergstrom bootstrap,
   see above): `add_clusters()` option to rerun n times with different seeds
   (`withr::local_seed()`) and return a co-assignment frequency per node, or a
   per-node "ambiguity" (how often it changes cluster); draw ambiguous nodes
   differently (transparency, or pie-like colours). Fits the "poles" idea:
   core nodes versus in-between nodes. Related to `merge_diagnostics()`.
5. **Inferential clustering as an alternative to Leiden.** SBM is in
   graph-tool (Python) in Peixoto's work; check whether an R option exists
   (packages to look up: `blockmodels`, `greed`, `randnet`, or the `sbm`
   package; none verified here) before promising anything. Python only if
   justified (see global conventions). At least document in the clustering
   guide that Leiden/modularity is descriptive and has a resolution limit and
   overfits (Peixoto 2023 on descriptive versus inferential).
6. **Null-model check of the map.** Peixoto/Jacomy both warn about seeing
   structure in noise: a helper drawing the same layout for a degree-preserving
   randomisation (`igraph::rewire()`, `keeping_degseq()`) beside the real
   network, to compare the visual clustering. Cheap and pedagogical.
7. **Standard of presentation.** Jacomy's blog "A standard for presenting
   network visualizations" and "Stop stretching your T-SNE, UMAP, and
   networks!" (titles only, not read): ideas for a caption helper (layout,
   parameters, size and colour meaning, filter applied, number of nodes and
   edges kept) and caution on our UMAP layout (distances not comparable
   between maps, no stretching).

### Ideas for the guide "Drawing networks" (`vignettes/articles/drawing-networks.qmd`)

The guide ends with a short "What comes next". Add a section **"The hairball
and what to do about it"** between "Comparing the layouts" and "Colours and
labels":

- What the layout encodes: locality, not groups (Jacomy; Venturini et al. 2021
  is already cited in the bib), gaps and Gestalt proximity, with a planted
  partition example (toy network with P_in decreasing, our own FR/FA2/UMAP).
- Three remedies, with the same network: (i) look with colours and reruns
  (Jacomy), (ii) prune before drawing (backbone, Nocaj, Dianati), (iii) make
  the layout obey a clustering (Peixoto).
- What a layout cannot show: disassortative structure (bipartite example),
  and the risk of apophenia: draw a randomised version.
- Say clearly that the three authors disagree (see above) and that the choice
  depends on whether the map is exploratory (Jacomy) or a figure for a paper
  (Peixoto: state the model).
- Link with `build_network(method = "sdsm")`: backbones can be applied before
  the layout through the projection itself.

## Approximate kNN projection (UMAP-like) for very large corpora, to test before any integration

Noted 2026-11-12. Nothing implemented.

- **Idea.** Instead of enumerating all coupled pairs as
  `biblio_coupling()` does (cost about $\sum_k n_k^2$, with $n_k$ the number
  of documents citing reference $k$), build a graph of the k nearest
  neighbours in cosine on the sparse document × reference incidence matrix
  (`uwot::similarity_graph()` or `rnndescent`), then compute the exact
  biblionetwork measure (coupling angle / strength / similarity) only on the
  pairs kept. Leiden and the rest of networkflow do not change.
- **Speed test.** Time and memory of `biblio_coupling()` against kNN on
  corpora of increasing size (10k, 50k, 200k, 800k documents); find the size
  at which exact coupling becomes impractical.
- **Quality test.** Compare the Leiden clusters of the two networks (adjusted
  Rand index, overlap of clusters) and their stability across seeds (kNN is
  not deterministic with several threads).
- **Caveats.** kNN caps degrees and removes isolated nodes, so it changes the
  nature of the network, not only the cost. On discrete data such as JEL
  codes, documents with the same set of codes make the choice of neighbours
  arbitrary (deduplicate first).
- **Criterion.** Add this layer to the package only if kNN is clearly faster
  at comparable cluster quality.

## From the verification on real data (2026-11-04)

Samples: Scopus (Journal of Monetary Economics, 1,865 documents; random
30,000 documents) and Web of Science (30,000 economics articles, 1990-2004).
Scripts in `bench/verification/`.

### To decide

- (Done 2026-11-05: `cluster_id` and `graphs` everywhere, `extract_tfidf()` keeps `data`. `weights` and `roles` in `add_node_roles()`.)

### Speed and memory

- ForceAtlas2 in pure R: all pairs at each iteration, about 1 minute for 1,000
  nodes and 4-5 for 2,000. A Barnes-Hut version needs compiled code (Rcpp) or an
  existing package (none on CRAN).
- UMAP: the shortest paths from every node (igraph::distances by blocks)
  dominate (75 s on 9,600 nodes): a k-nearest-neighbour search with a cutoff
  (Dijkstra stopped after k nodes) would be much faster.
- `layout_networks(compute_dynamic_coordinates = TRUE)` with `"fr"`: igraph
  drops its grid approximation when coordinates are given (80 s instead of 1 s
  on 9,600 nodes). Lower `niter` by default when coordinates are given?
- Backbones: `"sdsm"` about 20 s and 2 GB for 1,000 documents; `"fdsm"` does
  not finish with the default trials of backbone (documented, and a message).
- biblionetwork: `methods::as()` conversions take 20% of a coupling
  (`sparse_pairs()`), see biblionetwork.
- `merge_dynamic_clusters()`: about 20 ms per window of small data.table
  operations (one thread); a vectorised matching over all windows would
  make `merge_diagnostics()` faster.
- walktrap and infomap: minutes on networks of 10,000 nodes, with hundreds of
  clusters per window: document as such?

### Messages and checks

- Windows with very few nodes at the start or the end of the period (Scopus has
  documents dated 1892 or 2026): a message listing the number of nodes per
  window, or a warning for windows of fewer than n nodes.
- `layout_networks()` without `node_id`: R error ("argument missing"), could
  be a cli message.
